item.title: Body of former Chinese vice premier Liu Yandong cremated
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
Xi Jinping shakes hands with a family member of Liu Yandong to express deep condolences in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 3, 2026. The body of Liu Yandong, a former Chinese vice premier and state councilor, was cremated in Beijing on Tuesday. President Xi Jinping and other senior leaders of the Communist Party of China and the state, including Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi and Han Zheng, bid Liu farewell at the Babaoshan Revolutionary Cemetery on Tuesday morning. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi)
BEIJING, Nov. 3 (Xinhua) -- The body of Liu Yandong, a former Chinese vice premier and state councilor, was cremated in Beijing on Tuesday. She died of illness in Beijing on Oct. 28 at the age of 81.
President Xi Jinping and other senior leaders of the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the state, including Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi and Han Zheng, bid Liu farewell at the Babaoshan Revolutionary Cemetery on Tuesday morning.
Amid mournful strains of funeral music, they stood in silent tribute before Liu's remains and paid their final respects with three bows. They shook hands with Liu's family members to offer their condolences.
Liu had also served as a member of the Political Bureau of the 17th and 18th CPC Central Committees, and as vice chairperson of the 10th National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, China's top political advisory body.
She was extolled as an excellent Party member, a time-tested and loyal communist fighter, and an outstanding leader in the CPC's united front work and in the fields of education, science and technology, health, and work for women and children in China.
Xi Jinping, Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi, Han Zheng and Hu Jintao, among others, had either visited Liu while she was in the hospital or expressed deep condolences over her passing and offered sincere sympathies to her family members through various means.

item.title: Chinese premier calls for people-centered internet development amid AI advances
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
Chinese Premier Li Qiang delivers a keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit in Wuzhen, east China's Zhejiang Province, Nov. 3, 2026. Li attended the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit and delivered a keynote speech here on Tuesday. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen)
HANGZHOU, Nov. 3 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Tuesday called for a more people-centered approach to internet development amid rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI).
Li made the remarks in a keynote speech delivered at the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit in Wuzhen, east China's Zhejiang Province, on Tuesday morning.
Highlighting that the World Internet Conference has been held for 13 consecutive years, Li stressed that, despite rapid technological advances, one major question of common concern remains unchanged, namely how to make the internet better serve humanity.
Li said the internet is undergoing an intelligent transformation and a systemic leap as it increasingly integrates with AI and other technologies.
Stressing the need to place greater emphasis on a people-centered approach to internet development in today's world, Li said the ultimate purpose must be to promote the all-round development of people. He emphasized that internet-related technologies should enhance human capabilities, expand choices, affirm human value and improve well-being, rather than make humans subordinate to technology or exacerbate disparities in human development.
Calling for joint efforts to build a community with a shared future in cyberspace, Li said China will continue to pursue innovation through openness, promote technology transfer and knowledge sharing, and work with other countries to foster an open, inclusive and dynamic digital innovation ecosystem.
On digital security, Li said China will respect the legitimate cybersecurity concerns of all other countries and work together with them to address security challenges, while opposing the creation of a "digital iron curtain."
Li also pledged that China will actively implement the Global Development Initiative and support Global South countries in building digital infrastructure and enhancing their digital technology capabilities.
About 1,800 participants, including government officials, representatives of international organizations such as the United Nations and global internet companies, as well as experts and scholars, attended the opening ceremony.
Following the opening, Li visited the Light of Internet Expo and Wuzhen's World Internet Science and Technology Museum.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang visits the Light of Internet Expo and Wuzhen's World Internet Science and Technology Museum following the opening of the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit, in Wuzhen, east China's Zhejiang Province, Nov. 3, 2026. Li attended the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit and delivered a keynote speech here on Tuesday. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen)

item.title: China's central bank to raise forex reserve requirement ratio to keep yuan stable
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
BEIJING, Nov. 3 (Xinhua) -- China's central bank on Tuesday announced that it will raise the foreign exchange (forex) reserve requirement ratio for financial institutions by 2 percentage points, the first increase in nearly five years, in a move that is expected to ease the upward pressure on the Chinese currency renminbi and stabilize market expectations.
The People's Bank of China (PBOC) said in a statement that it will raise the forex reserve requirement ratio from 4 to 6 percent from Nov. 15 this year.
A macro-prudential management tool in the forex market, the forex reserve requirement ratio refers to the share of foreign currency deposits that financial institutions must hold at the PBOC. An increase tightens U.S. dollar liquidity and eases upward pressure on the renminbi, or the yuan, and a cut eases downward pressure on the yuan.
The latest move comes as the yuan has broadly strengthened this year. In the first nine months of this year, the yuan appreciated by a cumulative 4.2 percent against the U.S. dollar. The pace has accelerated since October, with the onshore yuan exchange rate strengthening for 14 consecutive trading days from October 14.
Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank, said that the increase in the ratio will help promote supply-demand balance in the forex market and curb a self-fulfilling cycle in which expectations of yuan appreciation drive further gains in the yuan.
He noted that raising the ratio is an open and transparent market-based measure, and that the adjustment sends a policy signal to the market that the central bank will stabilize market expectations and keep the yuan exchange rate basically stable at a reasonable and balanced level.
The PBOC has adjusted the ratio multiple times. In 2021, it raised the ratio twice to 9 percent. From 2022 to 2023, it lowered the ratio three times to the current 4 percent.
Following the announcement, the offshore yuan exchange rate fell against the U.S. dollar. Data from the China Foreign Exchange Trade System showed that as of 4:30 p.m., the onshore yuan spot exchange rate closed at 6.6765 against the U.S. dollar, weakening by 307 pips from the previous trading day.
In October, the PBOC issued its policy stance on the yuan exchange rate, saying that it will focus on preventing sharp short-term fluctuations in the exchange rate, especially sharp short-term depreciation that could affect financial stability.
The PBOC does not preset a target level for the exchange rate, but if the exchange rate fluctuates sharply in the short term and the market shows herd behavior and irrational expectations, it will introduce market-based measures to prevent short-term disruptive overshooting of the exchange rate, it said.
Ming Ming, chief economist at CITIC Securities, said the PBOC's move will freeze about 20 billion to 25 billion U.S. dollars of forex liquidity at the bank level and promote supply-demand balance in the domestic forex market.

item.title: U.S.-Iran tensions persist as midterms unfold, regional mediation continues
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
TEHRAN/WASHINGTON, Nov. 3 (Xinhua) -- With U.S. midterm elections beginning Tuesday, tensions between Washington and Tehran remained high as both sides exchanged warnings and conditions for a possible settlement, while regional countries stepped up diplomatic efforts to prevent renewed hostilities.
This photo taken on June 20, 2026 shows the Strait of Hormuz near Khasab, a small town in northern Oman. (Xinhua/Wen Xinnian)
IRAN WARNS AGAINST NEW ATTACKS, REITERATES DEMANDS
Chief of Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces Ali Abdollahi warned Tuesday that Iran's armed forces would respond to any level or type of threat from the United States and Israel immediately and "without geographical limitations."
Meanwhile, Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei said in a post on social media platform X that the U.S. response to Iran's demands was not convincing.
"They must completely and explicitly address Iran's seven conditions and act upon them. Only in this case the Strait of Hormuz will be reopened," Rezaei said.
Iran conveyed a plan to the United States through mediators on Sept. 22 to end hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if its conditions were met.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday that Iran had reduced the period for implementing the seven-day plan to two days in good faith.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei attends a weekly press conference in Tehran, Iran, Oct. 26, 2026. (Xinhua/Shadati)
TRUMP WEIGHS OPTIONS
U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday that he was "in no rush" to decide whether to resume military action against Iran.
"One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," Trump said in a phone interview with Axios.
Trump later wrote on Truth Social that Iran wanted a settlement and that one could happen soon.
Axios reported that Trump was weighing three possible courses of action: reaching a diplomatic deal, resuming military action, or maintaining maximum economic pressure without a deal or renewed hostilities.
U.S. Vice President JD Vance and White House envoy Steve Witkoff favor diplomacy, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth are pushing for renewed military operations. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State Marco Rubio favor maintaining the current "no war, no deal" status quo, the report said.
The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported Monday that Trump was leaning toward launching a large-scale attack on Iran after the midterm elections, potentially targeting Iranian infrastructure and nuclear facilities, although no final decision had been made.
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to the press on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., the United States, on May 1, 2026. (Photo by Li Yuanqing/Xinhua)
REGIONAL COUNTRIES STEP UP MEDIATION EFFORTS
Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said Tuesday that the United States and Iran were reviewing proposals to end their conflict, but differences remained unresolved.
He told a weekly press briefing that a Qatari delegation had returned from Tehran on Monday evening after more than three hours of talks with Iranian officials.
Qatar was relaying proposals in coordination with Pakistan, Gulf Cooperation Council countries and other regional and international partners, he said, adding that no concrete breakthrough had been achieved.
Also on Tuesday, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi urged the United States and Iran to show maximum flexibility and seek a political settlement.
At a joint press conference in Cairo with visiting Slovenian President Natasa Pirc Musar, he called on the two sides to "create space for understanding and dialogue" and pledged Egypt's continued efforts with regional and international partners to de-escalate tensions.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and his Iranian counterpart Seyed Abbas Araghchi made a phone call on Tuesday evening and discussed regional efforts to de-escalate tensions and reach a comprehensive deal addressing all parties' concerns, the Egyptian Foreign Ministry said.
This photo taken on June 30, 2026 shows a view of the Abdullah Bin Zaid Al Mahmoud Islamic Cultural Center in Doha, Qatar. (Photo by Nikku/Xinhua)
LIMITED U.S. STRIKES UNDERSCORE ESCALATION RISKS
Despite diplomatic efforts, military tensions have persisted.
The United States attacked Iran's strategic Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, The WSJ reported, citing U.S. officials.
Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps said late Monday that its air defense systems had intercepted three U.S. drones in the country's southern airspace, identifying two of them as MQM-170 Outlaw drones, which it said were intercepted over Qeshm Island, and the third as an MQ-9 Reaper, which it said was shot down in waters east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The strikes were part of a series of limited attacks Washington had secretly carried out against Iran in recent weeks while President Trump was touting the possibility of a diplomatic deal, the WSJ report said.
Washington did not publicly announce the strikes to avoid signaling a resumption of major combat operations, one U.S. official was quoted as saying.

item.title: New guardians carry forward age-old dialogue in China's Dunhuang
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04
* The 9th Silk Road (Dunhuang) International Cultural Expo opened in Dunhuang on Tuesday, gathering around 1,200 delegates from home and abroad with a focus on cultural exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations.
* Conservation technologies developed in Dunhuang have been rolled out to more than 150 heritage sites across China, and introduced to other countries including Kyrgyzstan and Myanmar.
* While heritage guardians tend to Dunhuang's ancient roots, creative innovators breathe new life into its timeless culture.
LANZHOU, Nov. 3 (Xinhua) -- Dunhuang, famed for its Mogao Caves, was a meeting place for diverse cultures along the ancient Silk Road. Today, it still draws people from far and wide, attracted by its renewed charm.
Yet the tales of cultural convergence stretch far beyond the expo's forums and exhibition halls, reaching into the daily rhythm of this oasis city, located in northwest China's Gansu Province. For many, Dunhuang is not merely a tourist attraction, but a second home where they build careers inspired by its age-old heritage. They, in turn, inject new energy into heritage preservation and cross-cultural exchange.
Some foreign guests at the expo remarked after touring the city that Dunhuang itself stands as a living example of dialogue between different cultures. Zoey Ashlyn Koehl, a student from Oklahoma City University in the United States, was impressed by the welcoming and dynamic vibe of Dunhuang: "I think it's a city open to all different kinds of people to come."
Participants select cultural and creative products at the 9th Silk Road (Dunhuang) International Cultural Expo in Dunhuang, northwest China's Gansu Province, Nov. 3, 2026. (Xinhua/Lang Bingbing)
SAFEGUARDING HERITAGE
Wu Shaoxia adjusted her equipment inside a cave as morning sunlight spilled over the cliff faces of the Mogao Caves. As a cultural relics photographer, she has been based in Dunhuang for 11 years.
Now 35 and originally from Shaanxi Province, also in northwest China, Wu is part of the Dunhuang Academy's digital team, featuring many young members from across China.
Wu regularly works inside the dim caves, repeating high-precision image capturing endeavors. Notably, she believes that "conservation is not only about rescuing endangered relics, but also racing against time to pass on the millennia-old beauty to future generations."
The young cultural workers in Dunhuang carry forward a mission begun decades ago. Over 80 years ago, a batch of heritage workers trekked into the Gobi Desert in a grottoes' conservation and research quest.
While their forerunners initially cleared sand from caves by hand and restored relics with simple tools, later generations have witnessed the evolution of conservation approaches.
So far, the academy has completed high-precision digital documentation of 323 caves, while its online digital library reunites Dunhuang manuscripts scattered around the world. Notably, as part of the Mogao Caves visitor experience, a dome film that immerses viewers as if inside the real grottoes draws on the academy's digital records.
"Earlier generations safeguarded the physical grottoes. We strive to preserve the look of this 1,000-year-old treasure," said Wu.
A staff member stitches mural images on a computer at the Dunhuang Academy in Dunhuang, northwest China's Gansu Province, April 25, 2023. (Xinhua/Chen Bin)
REIMAGINING TRADITIONS
Chen Lisong first visited Dunhuang ten years ago, instantly captivated by the depth of its ancient history.
Previously based in Shanghai in east China, she relocated to Dunhuang the following year and opened a souvenir shop. The designs of her products draw on iconic Mogao motifs, including the nine-colored deer and flying apsaras.
Chen later developed a Silk Road-themed dining space, where visitors can taste signature dishes from different regions along the ancient trade route.
For her, Dunhuang culture is not limited to cave murals. It can be woven into dining, accommodation and travel experiences. "Through modern design, it can be transformed into items people can take home," she said.
Shen Hongjie, a wood-carving artist, moved from central China's Hunan Province to Dunhuang in 2004, attracted by murals in the Mogao Caves and the local desert landscapes. He set up a studio, blending oil painting and traditional Chinese painting techniques with wood carving to recreate classic Mogao imagery.
In the early years of his venture, Dunhuang's cultural tourism sector remained nascent, with limited sales channels for his artworks. As local cultural tourism flourished in recent years, more visitors have poured into Shen's studio, while young apprentices have traveled from afar to learn the craft.
Dunhuang received some 24.39 million visitors in 2025, 3.7 times the number recorded in 2020. Cultural and creative products, immersive experiences and intangible heritage workshops are flourishing, appealing to culture-craving young Chinese.
This photo taken with a mobile phone shows Shen Hongjie, a wood-carving artist, making a woodcut in Dunhuang, northwest China's Gansu Province, May 10, 2023. (Xinhua/Ma Xiping)
BRIDGING CONTINENTS
Among those who fell for Dunhuang's charm are some cultural enthusiasts from overseas.
Ukrainian dancer Romanovych Inna and Georgian dancer Vaja Bukia settled in Dunhuang in 2024, and have performed in the dance drama "Ancient Sound of Dunhuang."
Discovering parallels between Georgian traditional dance and ancient Central Asian whirling dance movements depicted in Dunhuang's murals, Bukia incorporated his native dance elements into the show. "Both Georgia and Dunhuang carry ancient civilizations passed down for generations," he said.
For American researcher Neil Schmid, the first full-time foreign scholar at the Dunhuang Academy, his connection with Dunhuang began in the 1980s after reading a book on it.
He joined the academy in 2018 and has since shared Dunhuang's heritage globally via lectures, documentaries and publications. "The amazing thing about Dunhuang materials is that there is such a wealth," said Schmid.
The ongoing Dunhuang expo, first launched in 2016, further expands such exchanges. Referring to the ancient legacy of Dunhuang, Daren Tang, director-general of the World Intellectual Property Organization, said at the expo: "It reminds us that culture does not grow in isolation, but through exchange, new ideas and creativity."
Attending the expo for the second time, Hasebe Tsuyoshi, a professor from Japan's Kansai University who has been studying ancient Dunhuang music scores, said both the ancient and modern Dunhuang are crossroads of world cultures.
"Different civilizations have interwoven with one another since ancient times," he said, adding that it is important to continue such exchange and interaction.

item.title: China steps up monetary policy support to bolster stock market
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
This photo taken on Oct. 19, 2023 shows the People's Bank of China in Beijing, capital of China. (Xinhua/Peng Ziyang)
BEIJING, Nov. 3 (Xinhua) -- China will step up the use of monetary policy tools to support its capital market, strengthen market resilience and boost investor confidence, its central bank announced Monday.
The People's Bank of China (PBOC) said that it will conduct the third operation of the Securities, Funds and Insurance companies Swap Facility (SFISF) on Tuesday, aiming to help financial institutions secure funding and boost their capacity to buy stocks.
The operation will have a swap term of one year, with the possibility of extension depending on circumstances, according to the PBOC.
A total of 31 securities and fund companies have submitted applications for the facility, with the amount requested exceeding 100 billion yuan (about 14.89 billion U.S. dollars), the announcement said.
Introduced in October 2024, the SFISF allows eligible securities, fund and insurance companies to use assets, including bonds, stock exchange-traded funds and shares in companies on the CSI 300 Index, as collateral in exchange for highly liquid assets, such as treasury bonds and central bank bills. The facility is designed to improve participating institutions' access to funding and enhance their capacity to increase stock holdings.
Industry insiders believe the steady implementation of the swap facility will help put existing assets to better use, facilitate liquidity management across markets such as stocks and bonds, and provide a sustained flow of fresh liquidity to the capital market, thereby encouraging longer-term investment and strengthening the market's inherent stability.
In a statement released Monday, the PBOC said it had held a meeting with the National Financial Regulatory Administration and the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), calling for more effective use of the SFISF and the relending facility for share buybacks and shareholding increases.
The PBOC said it will conduct SFISF operations in a timely manner, expand the number of participating institutions, appropriately lower swap fees, and optimize the collateral and operational arrangements.
"We will work with the PBOC to guide relevant market participants in making full use of the two policy tools and coordinate efforts to support market stability," an official with the CSRC said in response to a media query.
The relending facility, launched in 2024 as a temporary measure, will become a long-term arrangement. Its relending rate will be cut from 1.25 percent to 1 percent. Financial institutions are to follow market-based pricing principles, set lending rates reasonably based on the relending rate, and expand lending under the facility.
The central bank conducted the previous two SFISF operations in October 2024 and January 2025, with a combined volume of 105 billion yuan, official data showed.
Meanwhile, loans for share buybacks and shareholding increases have reached about 440 billion yuan in signed agreements, with more than 280 billion yuan already disbursed, helping listed companies finance their market capitalization management activities.
The three departments will step up policy support to stabilize the capital market, strengthen its resilience and boost market confidence, while refining policy arrangements and implementation rules and encouraging financial institutions to make full use of the tools, according to the PBOC statement.
The CSRC official said the commission would expand the scope of the relending facility for share buybacks and shareholding increases by listed companies.
The CSRC will urge listed firms that have disclosed repurchase and share increase plans to accelerate implementation progress, and those that have applied for loans to intensify their repurchase efforts, thus sustaining the current sound momentum of stock repurchases and contributing to the stability of the capital market, it said.
"Stock repurchase is an important tool for listed companies to manage their market value, and a key means to stabilize stock prices and convey development prospects and confidence," the official said.
In the first 10 months of this year, 645 listed companies on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges disclosed 700 share repurchase plans totaling 237.7 billion yuan, with the amounts of planned repurchases and actual repurchases both hitting record highs, according to the CSRC.

item.title: Small producers, big markets -- the CIIE story
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02
This photo taken on Oct. 26, 2026 shows the south square of the National Exhibition and Convention Center (Shanghai), the main venue for the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), in east China's Shanghai. (Xinhua/Fang Zhe)
by Maya Majueran
At a time when global trade is increasingly disturbed by tariffs, protectionism and geopolitical competition, a different story is emerging from Shanghai's exhibition halls.
It is not about multinational giants or the strategic interests of major economies. It is about Peruvian artisans, Kenyan avocado farmers and Malagasy herders -- ordinary producers seeking access to international markets and opportunities to improve their livelihoods.
The China International Import Expo (CIIE) is helping turn "inclusive globalization" from a diplomatic slogan into economic reality by creating market opportunities, generating employment, and improving livelihoods.
For many developing countries, the greatest obstacle to international trade is not a lack of products or entrepreneurial ambition, but limited access to markets, financing, logistics and commercial networks. Through targeted support, dedicated exhibition areas for least-developed countries, and direct connections with Chinese buyers, the CIIE seeks to reduce these barriers.
The objective is not charity, but meaningful participation in global trade.
The CIIE's significance also lies in its continuity. Through its "6 days + 365 days" model, the expo connects temporary exhibitions with year-round trading platforms. Bonded warehousing, cross-border e-commerce, and buyer matchmaking help businesses turn initial orders into sustained commercial relationships.
In July 2025, Burundi shipped 38.4 tonnes of Arabica coffee directly to China for the first time, followed by contracts exceeding 900 tonnes worth over 5 million U.S. dollars.
A visitor learns about coffee at the pavilion of Burundi during the eighth China International Import Expo (CIIE) in east China's Shanghai, Nov. 7, 2025. (Xinhua/Ren Pengfei)
At the seventh CIIE in 2024, 13 of 16 participating Nigerian companies reportedly secured agreements, including a cocoa contract worth over 1.2 million dollars.
The eighth CIIE last year recorded 83.49 billion dollars in one-year intended deals, up 4.4 percent from the previous edition and hitting a new high.
Smaller economies face structural disadvantages in international trade. Regulatory compliance, logistics, marketing, and distribution impose disproportionately high costs on low-volume exporters. By connecting buyers and sellers and facilitating market entry, the CIIE helps reduce these barriers.
The CIIE offers one practical model for smaller economies to access international markets. For artisans in Peru, farmers in Kenya, and herding communities in Madagascar, the benefits can extend beyond export contracts to employment, household incomes and local development.
Inclusive globalization should be measured not simply by how much trade expands, but by how widely its opportunities are shared.
It is an approach worth drawing on.
